_doc: Frozen test cases for the spec-elaboration experiment. `request` is the vague incoming prompt an arm receives; it is all the arm ever sees. `nuances` is the HELD-OUT checklist: specific things a well-elaborated spec must name, written before any arm ran and never edited after reading an arm's output (score-predictions-as-registered). An arm's prompt never contains them and no subject call may read this file. `category` groups a nuance so a grade says which kind of nuance an arm misses.

categories.interaction: two parts of the request meeting each other, or the change meeting what exists
categories.edge: first, repeated, empty, largest, boundary values
categories.unhappy: wrong input, refusal, limit reached, a dependency failing
categories.async: work that does not finish in the request, its completion path and its retries
categories.data: what is stored, its shape, its identity, its retention
categories.permission: who may see or do what, and what must never widen
categories.operator: start, stop, configure, observe, recover, go back
categories.platform: a rule of the runtime the request is built on that binds the design
categories.nonfunctional: a bound, a latency, an interface quality
categories.preserve: existing behaviour the change must not break

cases.title: Grok bot in a Salesforce development org
cases.note: The owner's sample request, 2026-11-20. Greenfield on a platform with hard, well-documented limits: it tests whether elaboration reaches for runtime rules the request never mentions.
cases.request: Create a Grok bot in a Salesforce development org.

nuances.nuance: Which Salesforce surface the bot is invoked from (a Lightning record page component, the utility bar, Experience Cloud, a Flow action) and what context that surface hands it.
The bot answers only from records the asking user can already see: it runs in the user's sharing context and never widens record visibility.
Field-level security and encrypted or restricted fields are honoured in what the bot reads and shows.
Who may use the bot and who may administer it, expressed as a permission set or equivalent, not as 'everyone'.
One user's conversation is not readable by another user; an administrator's access to conversations is stated deliberately.
The model call is an external callout, so it cannot run synchronously from a trigger and cannot follow DML in the same transaction: the design is asynchronous (Queueable, future, or batch).
The API credential lives in a Named/External Credential or protected custom setting, never in code, metadata or a log.
Governor limits that bind this design are named with their numbers: callout timeout ceiling, callouts per transaction, heap, CPU time.
Apex tests cannot make real callouts, so the test approach requires a mock callout implementation.
The remote endpoint must be registered (Remote Site Setting or the Named Credential's host) or the callout is refused.
How the interface learns the answer arrived: a platform event, change data capture, a polled status field, or Lightning Message Service — not an assumption that the call returns inline.
A retried or re-enqueued async job must not post the same reply twice (idempotency on the message or request).
Queue depth or concurrent-job limits, and what happens to a request that cannot be enqueued.
The model API refusing (4xx), failing (5xx) and timing out each have a distinct, stated user-visible outcome.
Provider rate limiting or quota exhaustion: backoff, retry policy, and what the user is told.
A partial or truncated answer, and what the user sees when an answer never arrives.
The stored shape: a conversation and its turns as records, with role, text, status, timestamps, the model identifier and token or usage counts.
How long conversations are kept and how they are removed, including on user deletion.
What org data is assembled into the prompt, and the rule limiting it to what the asking user may see; personal data in prompts is addressed.
A conversation outgrowing the model's context window: what is trimmed or summarised, and at what size.
The first use (no history), an empty question, and an answer or question at the maximum accepted length.
An administrator can turn the bot off, change the model, and see failed requests.
An audit record of who asked what and what was answered, with its retention.

A development org is not production: how the configuration and credential differ per environment, and how the work is deployed (scratch org or sandbox, metadata deployment, the production code-coverage requirement).
A latency target or bound for an answer, and truthful in-progress feedback in the interface while the async work runs.
A deliberately designed interface: states for empty, loading, error and refused, not unstyled scaffolding.
Existing org behaviour is untouched: no new sharing, no change to existing records, no trigger that alters current flows.

cases.title: Waitlist for a class booking app
cases.note: A change to a product that exists, consumer-facing, concurrency-heavy. Tests whether elaboration finds the race and the policy interactions.
cases.request: Add a waitlist to our class booking app so full classes don't turn people away.

nuances.nuance: What happens when a spot opens: automatic promotion, or an offer the person must accept within a stated window.
The order the waitlist is served in (join time), how ties resolve, and whether any membership tier or staff override jumps the queue.
A person on the waitlist for two classes that overlap in time: promoting one must resolve the other.
The no-show or late-cancellation policy that already exists: whether a declined or missed promotion counts against it.
Promotion is triggered by a cancellation that happens outside the person's session, so it is background work with a stated trigger and timeliness.
Notification of a promotion: the channel, what it says, and what happens when sending fails.
Two spots opening at once, or two cancellations at the same moment: no double promotion and no over-booked class.
A waitlisted person booking directly at the same moment a promotion is offered to them.
Payment for a promoted booking: when it is taken and what happens when it fails.
A cap on the waitlist itself, and what a person sees when even the waitlist is full.
A cut-off before class start after which no promotion happens.
Staff raising or lowering a class's capacity while a waitlist exists.
The class being cancelled entirely: what happens to everyone waiting.
The waitlist entry as a record with its join time and state, and whether a position is stored or derived.
What becomes of waitlist entries after the class has run, and how long they are kept.
What a member can see of the waitlist: their own position, and not other people's identities.
Staff can see the waitlist, promote or remove someone by hand, and see who was promoted when.
The feature can be turned off, or enabled per class or class type.
A bound on how soon a promotion follows a cancellation.
A class that is not full still books directly as it does today, and existing bookings are unaffected.
Classes that are already full when the feature ships: whether they gain a waitlist and how.

cases.title: Automatic reminders for unpaid invoices
cases.note: Scheduled outbound work touching money and real recipients. Tests whether elaboration finds the backfill blow-up, the stop conditions and idempotency.
cases.request: Set up automatic reminders for unpaid invoices.

nuances.nuance: The schedule: how many reminders and at what offsets from the due date, including whether any are sent before it.
Every condition that stops the sequence: paid, part-paid, voided, credited, disputed, or on a payment plan.
A part-paid invoice: whether the reminder states the remaining balance rather than the original amount.
An existing do-not-contact, paused or unsubscribed state on the customer, and whether a billing notice is exempt from a marketing opt-out.
Idempotency: the same reminder is never sent twice, including after a retry, a redeploy or two schedulers running.
A check at the moment of sending that the invoice is still unpaid, not only when the batch was selected.
The send failing: retry policy, a provider outage, and escalation to a person when it keeps failing.
The sending provider's rate limit and how a large batch is paced within it.
Invoices already overdue when the feature is switched on: the whole backlog of reminders does not go out at once.
Time zone and sending hours: the customer's local time, business hours, weekends and holidays.
Currency and amount formatting for the recipient.
A bouncing or invalid recipient address, and an invoice with no contact at all.
More than one billing contact, and which of them is written to.
A record per invoice per reminder step, showing what was sent and when, visible on the invoice.
What the reminder contains: invoice reference, amount, due date and a way to pay, and whether that link expires.
Who may configure the schedule and who may send or stop a reminder by hand.
Turning it off globally and per customer, previewing or dry-running it, and resending by hand.
Seeing what the system will send next and what it failed to send.
A bound on sending volume or on how late a scheduled reminder may go out.
Nothing changes about how invoices are created, paid or recorded.

cases.title: Bulk-create users from an uploaded CSV
cases.note: File input, partial failure and a genuine privilege-escalation hole. Tests whether elaboration finds the security and partial-failure nuance.
cases.request: Let admins upload a CSV to bulk-create users.

nuances.nuance: Partial failure: whether the import is all-or-nothing or row by row, stated deliberately.
What the admin gets back: a result naming the rows that failed and why.
A row matching a user who already exists: skipped, updated, or an error — and duplicates within the one file.
An import must not create a user with more access than the importer has: roles named in the file are checked against the importer's own authority.
Who may import at all, and that the ability is not implied by being able to create one user.
Validation of the file itself: required columns, unexpected or missing columns, a missing header row.
File encoding and shape: a byte-order mark, line endings, quoted fields containing commas or newlines.
A row failing after side effects have already happened for earlier rows (invitations already sent).
A limit on file size or row count, and what happens to a file above it.
An empty file, a file with only a header, and a single-row file.
The same file uploaded twice: the import is idempotent or says why not.
A large file is processed in the background, and how the admin learns it finished.
The new users' invitation or welcome mail: whether hundreds go out at once, and the pacing if so.
The initial state of a created user: active or pending, with or without a password, and how they first sign in.
The uploaded file holds personal data: where it is stored, for how long, and who may download it again.
Date, number and locale handling of the file's values.
An audit of who imported what and when.
Cancelling an import that is running, and retrying only the rows that failed.
A bound on how long a file of the stated maximum size takes, and visible progress while it runs.
Creating a single user by hand still works exactly as it does, and existing users are not modified.
Hostile content in the file: a value that becomes a formula when the result is opened in a spreadsheet, or a field far longer than any column allows.
